extracted.intended_audience: researchers of peer review, funding agency staff, and grant program designers
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying the criteria reviewers use to evaluate grant proposals and the procedural variables of panel decision‑making that shape funding outcomes. Useful for designing review rubrics and review procedures in research funding agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific quality / merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific quality / merit of the proposal
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly cited core criterion; reviewers differ in how they interpret and weigh scientific quality. Often invoked as the central evaluation dimension but its relative importance varies across panels and reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / innovativeness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates novelty of ideas or approaches. Some reviewers prioritize high-risk/high-innovation work while others penalize lack of proven track record; weight given to originality varies by reviewer and by decision procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses whether the proposed work can realistically be completed given methods, timeline, and resources. Feasibility judgments interact with perceived risk and applicant track record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant qualifications / track record
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considers the PI's past achievements, publication record, and demonstrated capacity to deliver. Strong track record can compensate for higher risk; lack of track record can reduce chances under consensus procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality and appropriateness of the proposed methods. Methodological rigor is a distinct focus for some reviewers and may be assessed separately from overall scientific merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic / mission relevance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fit with the funder’s goals, programme priorities, or strategic agenda. Reviewers and panels vary in how much they let mission relevance outweigh scientific or methodological concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-effectiveness / budget reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of whether the proposed budget is reasonable given the aims and likely outputs. Becomes especially salient when panels face hard budget caps and must triage on cost–benefit grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rating scale design
rubrics_metrics.description: Rating scale design (granular numeric vs. categorical labels vs. 'fund/no-fund' binary)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The design of the rating scale strongly shapes outcomes: more granular numeric scales can differentiate proposals finely; categorical or binary scales push coarser decisions. Choice of scale interacts with aggregation method and can advantage different proposal types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget restrictions (panel-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Budget restrictions: panels with hard caps vs. those without
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard caps force panels to triage and prioritize cost-effectiveness, favoring lower-cost or higher 'value' proposals. Panels without caps can recommend riskier or more costly projects, sometimes deferring budget constraints to higher administrative levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking method (aggregation/decision procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ranking method: averaging individual scores vs. consensus discussion vs. comparative ranking
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different aggregation/decision procedures produce different winners: consensus-based processes tend to fund safer, less controversial proposals; averaging individual scores tends to favor proposals with broad moderate enthusiasm; comparative ranking emphasizes direct pairwise judgments and can produce different distributions of risk and innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighting/prioritization of criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative weight assigned to each criterion varies dramatically by reviewer and panel
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no fixed weighting scheme across reviewers; some prioritize methodological rigor, others mission relevance or applicant track record. This variability means identical proposals can be scored very differently depending on who reviews them and which weights are implicit in the panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural design as determinant of outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision procedures (rating scales, budget constraints, ranking methods) have larger effects on funding outcomes than written review guidelines
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: changing procedures changes which proposals win more than changing written criteria. Therefore, reforms aimed at improving fairness or enabling innovation should prioritize procedure design (scale choice, aggregation rule, budget handling) over solely revising evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit values embedded in decision procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Each decision procedure carries implicit values: consensus = stability, averaging = moderation, ranking = comparison
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting a procedure implicitly selects for certain values (e.g., stability vs. risk-taking). Panel and funder design choices should be explicit about which values they want to promote, because procedure choice will steer portfolio composition.
